My posting queue was completely full and starving at the same time.

200 slots, every one of them spoken for, and it was putting out 2.4 posts a day. My first instinct was that I had outgrown the tool and needed to pay for more room.

I had not. I had committed the slots too far forward.

A post scheduled for October 31 holds its slot from the day you make it. Sitting there in early September, that is 53 days of capacity spent on 1 post. Do that a hundred times and the tool is full while the next 2 weeks sit nearly empty.

The fix cost nothing. Hold about 12 days at a time and keep everything past that in a backlog you refill as things publish. Same 200 slots, 7 times the daily output.

The general version, which is the part I actually want to remember:

When a resource looks maxed out, check how far ahead you have committed it before you go buy more of it. Capacity problems and scheduling problems look identical from the outside, and only one of them costs money to solve.

I explained the same rule 3 times and it was still applied wrong. That was my fault, not theirs.

The rule was simple. A specific number of posts per account per day. I said it, I repeated it, I said it more sharply the third time.

Then I went and looked at the tool that was supposed to enforce it, and the tool had no field for which account a post belonged to. It could not tell 2 accounts apart. So it was counting a full day across 4 channels as one oversized pile and flagging a correct day as a mistake.

No amount of me repeating myself was ever going to fix that. The rule was unenforceable in the shape the data was in.

The lesson I keep relearning:

If you have had to say something twice, stop saying it. Go find the missing field, the missing column, the missing check. Repetition is what we reach for when we have not yet found the thing that made the instruction impossible to follow.

Guidance governs judgment. When judgment is not the thing that failed, guidance is not the fix.

Every Tuesday, 1 thing I learned the hard way. No theory, just the receipts.

Someone told me a thing I owned did not exist.

Every default view is somebody's opinion about what you probably want. Your analytics has a default date range. Your inbox has a default sort. Your file browser quietly hides the folders it decided are not for you. None of that is malicious, and all of it is invisible, because a filtered view does not look filtered. It looks like the whole thing.

So when a tool tells you something is not there, the useful question is not why is it missing. It is what is this view choosing not to show me.

I lose more time to that than to anything that is actually broken.

The panic was a story about a story.

In 1938 Orson Welles read War of the Worlds on the radio and America supposedly lost its mind. It did not. The audience that night was small, and researchers who went back to the ratings found no evidence of mass hysteria.

Newspapers were losing advertising to radio and had every reason to make radio look dangerous.

So they wrote the panic.
